summary: Describes RANGER, an architectural framework for scalable routing and addressing in networks with global enterprise recursion. An "enterprise" here can range from a small home office network to a multi-organizational corporation, or even the global Internet itself, and the framework nests them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RANGER describes how to build a network out of networks. Each organisation keeps its own addressing plan, and traffic between them travels through tunnels, so the same private addresses can be reused in different parts of the structure.

questions: how can routing scale with enterprise networks
what is the difference between an eid and an rloc
subtitle: A framework for networks built out of networks, with separate addresses for identity and location.

tldr.problem: The global routing table is growing faster than it can be carried, and the same addresses cannot be reused between organisations, so an enterprise that contains other enterprises has no agreed way to arrange its routing and addressing.
tldr.mechanism: RANGER separates the address a host is reached at from the address of the router that reaches it, and links enterprises together with tunnels so that each enterprise can keep its own addressing plan, including reusing the same private addresses in different parts of the tree.
tldr.outcome: The document sets out the architecture, the mechanisms it is built from, and the cases it is meant to cover: autoconfiguration, provider-independent addressing, mobility, multihoming, border router discovery and tunnel MTU.

facts.label: Two address spaces
facts.value: Routing locator space and endpoint identifier space

today: RFC 5720 is an Informational Independent Submission published in February 2010, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an architecture rather than a protocol, and the document notes that related work was under way at the time in the IRTF Routing Research Group and in IETF working groups.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RANGER is an architectural framework for scalable routing and addressing in networks with global enterprise recursion. The term enterprise network here covers a wide range of use cases, from a small office or home network to a mobile ad hoc network, a multi-organizational corporation, or the global Internet itself. Such networks need an architected solution for coordinating routing and addressing plans that accommodates scalability, provider-independence, mobility, multihoming and security. These considerations are especially true for existing deployments, but the same principles apply to clean-slate ones, and the architecture also provides a framework for IPv6 and IPv4 coexistence.

RANGER gives a unifying architecture for enterprises that contain one or more distinct interior IP routing and addressing domains, called routing locator space, with each such space containing one or more organizational groupings. Each space may coordinate its own internal addressing plan independently of the others, so limited-scope addresses such as private-use IPv4 addresses can be reused with impunity, giving unlimited scaling through spatial reuse. Each routing locator space therefore appears as an enterprise unto itself, and an enterprise can also be partitioned into sub-enterprises, or sites. Without an architected approach, routing and addressing inside such a structure would be fragmented by address reuse between disjoint enterprises. With RANGER, several enterprises can be linked to provide a multi-hop transit for nodes attached to edge networks that use endpoint identifier addresses taken from a range distinct from any routing locator space.

RANGER is recursive in that several enterprises can be joined in a nested enterprise-within-enterprise fashion, each connecting edge networks whose nodes use addresses from the endpoint identifier space to support separation of edge and core. The same principles extend upwards to parent enterprises and ultimately to the core of the global Internet. The document also raises the question of whether the global Internet is a limiting condition for recursion, and whether other internets could be manifested as parallel universes joined at still higher levels.

The architecture is carried out by composite technologies: Virtual Enterprise Traversal, the Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer, and ISATAP, with mechanisms such as IPsec also in scope. The issues it addresses, in whole or in part, are scalable routing and addressing, provider-independent addressing and its relation to provider-aggregated addressing, site mobility and multihoming, address and prefix autoconfiguration, border router discovery, tunnelling between routers and hosts and between hosts, neighbour discovery over tunnels, MTU determination for tunnels, and IPv6 and IPv4 coexistence and transition. The document uses IPv6 over IPv4 as its illustrative example, but says the same principles apply to any combination of one IP version as an overlay over another.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework has two ideas running through it. First, enterprises nest: an enterprise can contain smaller enterprises, and the global Internet is just the outermost one. Second, each enterprise keeps its own addresses, so two unrelated networks can both use 10.0.0.0/8 without colliding.

sections.title: The Vocabulary of RANGER
sections.content:
A routing locator is an IPv4 or IPv6 address assigned to an interface in an enterprise-interior routing region. Private-use addresses are local to each enterprise, so the same private-use addresses may appear within disjoint enterprises. An endpoint identifier is an address assigned to an edge network interface of an end system, and the endpoint identifier space must be separate and distinct from any routing locator space.

A commons is an enterprise-interior routing region that provides a subnetwork for cooperative peering between the border routers of diverse organisations that may have competing interests; the prime example is the default-free zone of the global Internet, and the addressing plan used inside it comes from routing locator space. An enterprise deploys a unified routing locator space addressing plan within the commons, but may also contain partitions with disjoint routing locator spaces and organisational groupings that count as enterprises in their own right. The principles apply to any network with some degree of cooperative active management, which extends the idea to home networks, small offices, provider networks, mobile ad hoc networks and the global Internet. A site is a grouping of interfaces within an enterprise commons whose topology is a proper subset of the enterprise's, and sites may contain interior sites in the same recursive way. At the lowest level of decomposition, a single border router can be considered an enterprise unto itself.

An enterprise border router is a router at the edge of an enterprise that is also configured as a tunnel endpoint in an overlay network. It connects its directly attached networks to the overlay and reaches other networks by IP-in-IP tunnelling across the commons to other border routers. An enterprise border gateway is a border router that also connects the enterprise to provider networks or to the global Internet; it is typically configured as a default router in the overlay and provides forwarding for IP networks not reachable through a border router inside the commons. An ingress tunnel endpoint is a host or router interface that encapsulates inner IP packets in an outer IP header for transmission over the enterprise-interior routing region to the routing locator of an egress tunnel endpoint, and an egress tunnel endpoint receives such packets, decapsulates them and delivers them to the endpoint identifier of the final destination. An overlay network is a virtual network manifested by routing and addressing over virtual links formed through automatic tunnelling, and it may span many underlying enterprises.

A provider-independent prefix is an endpoint identifier prefix that is routable within a limited scope and may also appear in enterprise mapping tables; such prefixes are typically delegated to a border router by a registry but are not aggregated by a provider network, and local-use prefixes are another example even though they usually do not appear in mapping tables. A provider-aggregated prefix is an endpoint identifier prefix derived from a provider-independent prefix or delegated directly to a provider network by a registry; a prefix taken from a delegating router's provider-independent space becomes provider-aggregated from the point of view of the requesting router.
sections.plainLanguage: Two address spaces sit side by side. A routing locator says where a router is and is what the network routes on. An endpoint identifier says which host is meant and is only meaningful locally. Everything else in the vocabulary describes the roles the routers play in the nesting.

sections.title: Routing and Addressing: Map and Encaps
sections.content:
The Internet faces growing pains, with indications that core routing information base scaling may not be sustainable over the long term and that the remaining space for IPv4 address allocations may be depleted in the near future. The same solutions chosen for the global Internet can apply to large enterprises, or to any enterprise that would benefit from separating its core and edge addressing domains.

RANGER supports scalable routing through an approach that parallels the New Scheme for Internet Routing and Addressing described in RFC 1955, commonly known as map-and-encaps. An ingress tunnel endpoint that must forward a packet first consults a mapping system to find the mapping from the destination's endpoint identifier to the routing locator of an egress tunnel endpoint. The mapping system is typically a per-enterprise distributed database synchronised among a limited set of mapping agents; alternatives include a routing protocol instance maintained by border gateways and a DNS reverse zone distributed among a restricted set of caching servers. Entries are inserted by administrative configuration, automated prefix registrations and similar means.

The ingress tunnel endpoint may either consult the mapping system itself, delaying or dropping the first packets, or forward those first packets to a border gateway acting as a default mapper. Either way it receives a mapping reply it can use to populate its forwarding information base, and the choice between the two depends on the enterprise scenario: forwarding to a border gateway may suit some, self-discovery others. Other mapping mechanisms are possible.

Once the mapping is known, the ingress tunnel endpoint encapsulates inner packets in an outer IP header for transmission across the commons to the routing locator of the egress tunnel endpoint, which decapsulates them and forwards them towards the endpoint identifier of the destination. The consequence is that the routing information base within the commons only holds state about routing locators, not endpoint identifiers, while the synchronised endpoint-identifier-to-routing-locator state lives in a smaller number of nodes and does not oscillate when link state changes inside the commons. Endpoint identifiers are routable only within a limited scope in edge networks, which may be as small as a single node.

Scalable addressing follows from choosing a suitably large endpoint identifier range that is kept distinct from the enterprise-interior routing locator ranges. Taking endpoint identifier space from the IPv6 addressing architecture therefore gives a viable and scalable alternative, while taking it from the already exhausted IPv4 architecture may not.
sections.plainLanguage: Before forwarding, a node asks a mapping system which router can reach the destination host. It then wraps the packet in an outer header addressed to that router. The network itself only ever routes on router addresses, so the host addresses never have to appear in the global routing table.

sections.title: Enterprises Within Enterprises
sections.content:
Enterprise networks traditionally distribute routing information with interior gateway protocols such as OSPF, while large enterprises may even use an exterior gateway protocol internally in place of one. It is becoming common for large enterprises to use BGP internally, independently of the BGP instance that maintains the routing information base within the global Internet's default-free zone. A large enterprise may therefore run an internal BGP instance across many internal autonomous systems and appear as an internet unto itself, with default routes leading to the real Internet; each internal autonomous system may itself run BGP internally and appear as an independent, lower-tier enterprise.

The example in the document shows enterprise E1 connected to the global Internet through routers R1 to Rn, alongside other enterprises E2 to EN that also connect to the global Internet. Within the E1 commons there may be many hosts, routers and networks using routing locator addresses, over which both encapsulated and unencapsulated packets are forwarded. There may also be lower-tier enterprises, E1.1 to E1.m, that interconnect inside the E1 commons through border routers X1 to X9, which in turn see R1 to Rn as border gateways. Within each of those there may be further lower-tier enterprises interconnecting through border routers Y1 to Y9, which see X1 to X9 as border gateways. The decomposition nests as deeply as desired and ultimately terminates at single nodes, which may be simple hosts or border routers attaching complex edge networks with endpoint identifier addresses, from a home network behind a residential gateway to a corporate or academic campus.

From the highest level, the global Internet can itself be viewed as an enterprise interconnecting lower-tier enterprises, so that all the RANGER principles apply equally there. The architecture does not treat the global Internet as a limiting condition for recursion, allowing other internets to be manifested as parallel universes joined at still higher levels.

The document gives one concrete case. The future global Aeronautical Telecommunications Network, under consideration in the civil aviation industry, will take the form of a large enterprise network that appears as an internet unto itself, with many air communications and air navigation service provider networks organised as autonomous systems internal to it. Their border gateways will take part in a BGP instance internal to the network and may run independent BGP instances of their own, further divided into lower-tier enterprises. Those providers share a common objective of safety of flight, but there may be competing business, social and political interests between them, so the network is not one big happy family, and the model parallels the global Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The structure is like a set of Russian dolls. A large organisation runs its own interior routing between its sites, which can in turn run theirs, and at the top the global Internet does the same thing for everyone. Because the nesting is recursive, the same rules apply at every level.

sections.title: Virtual Enterprise Traversal, SEAL, Mobility and Multihoming
sections.content:
Within the enterprise-within-enterprise framework, the architecture is based on overlay networks manifested through Virtual Enterprise Traversal, which uses automatic IP-in-IP tunnelling: ingress tunnel endpoints encapsulate endpoint-identifier-based inner packets in routing-locator-based outer headers for transmission across the commons to egress tunnel endpoints. For each enterprise they connect to, border routers using VET configure a non-broadcast, multiple access interface known as a VET interface, which sees all other border routers in the enterprise as potential single-hop neighbours from the point of view of the inner IP protocol. Standard neighbour discovery mechanisms such as router advertisements and redirects can then be used between border router pairs, giving a data-driven model in which neighbour relationships form on traffic demand, which in many cases relaxes the need for dynamic routing exchanges in the control plane. Where several VET interfaces are linked, traversal is seen as several VET hops, and moving between interfaces means decapsulating and re-encapsulating, so a traceroute would show one inner forwarding hop per interface crossed.

Within this framework, border routers in lower-tier enterprises coordinate their endpoint identifier prefixes with the border gateways of an upper-tier enterprise. Provider-aggregated prefixes are delegated down the hierarchy: a border gateway delegating 2001:DB8::/40 may delegate /48 to the next tier down, which delegates /52, which delegates /56, with DHCP prefix delegation as the preferred mechanism, which also arranges for the prefixes to be published in the enterprise routing system. Provider-independent prefixes are registered instead by the border router itself, which sends router advertisements to the border gateways in its enterprise to assert ownership, optionally signed with the mechanisms of SEcure Neighbor Discovery. The gateways verify the sender's credentials, register the prefixes in the enterprise mapping system, and forward a proxied advertisement to the gateways of their parent enterprises, and so on up the hierarchy until a default-free commons is reached. The owner must then send further advertisements periodically to refresh the expiry timers.

The document works through an end-to-end example: a host nested deep inside enterprise E1 attaches to a dual-stack router that advertises IPv6 prefixes and is discovered by ordinary IPv6 neighbour discovery as a default router. That router sees the next border gateway as reachable over a VET interface, and so on up the chain until a border router connects E1 to the global Internet. In a second example, when a packet arrives for a peer in another organisational entity and the receiving border router has no matching forwarding entry, it can do an on-demand mapping lookup against the enterprise mapping service, or forward the packet to a default router that redirects it, after which the border router can prove to the next hop that it is allowed to send packets with that source prefix and forward directly from then on. Dynamic routing and on-demand mapping can be used as complements, or either alone.

Legacy hosts, routers and networks that were already numbered with routing locator addresses must keep working for the long term. A legacy IPv4-only node behind address translation must still reach legacy IPv4-only services long after endpoint-identifier services are widely deployed. A legacy client can reach a legacy server inside the same enterprise with no encapsulation at all, by looking up a mapping in the enterprise-local name service. To reach a legacy server on the public Internet, either all nested enterprises share one routing locator space, in which case normal IPv4 forwarding works and the outermost gateway acts as a translator or an ordinary border router; or the nested enterprises use disjoint routing locator spaces, in which case the outermost gateway can act as a carrier-grade translator and the innermost border router can carry packets to it inside an IPv4-in-IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnel; or the client can be configured as an endpoint-identifier node and use standard IPv6 routing to reach a translator at the border router of the enterprise where the server lives; or the two ends can implement protocol translation themselves.

Three further areas are covered. The Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer gives every encapsulated packet a monotonically incrementing 32-bit identification field that tunnel endpoints can use as a nonce to detect off-path spoofing, lets endpoints keep working when many ICMP messages are lost, and lets them adapt to subnets whose links have different maximum transmission units. For mobility, nomadic devices that do not need session continuity can simply be renumbered; devices with provider-independent prefixes can move between attachment points by withdrawing their prefixes from the mapping systems of the enterprises they leave and injecting them into the new ones, and a carefully arranged hierarchy can damp the resulting churn; devices that move quickly between unrelated attachment points should use provider-aggregated addresses coordinated through a rendezvous service, and mechanisms such as Mobile IPv6 or the Host Identity Protocol can keep a stable identifier while they move. The example given is an aircraft with a mobile router moving between ground stations: if the stations are within the same enterprise or lower-tier sites of one parent enterprise, the aircraft only announces its prefixes at the new point and withdraws them from the old, and there is no aircraft-wide readdressing event. For multihoming, border routers can register their provider-independent prefixes with several border gateways and use them in a fault-tolerant and load-balancing way; a corporation with several providers can register its prefixes with all of them and use any of them, and an aircraft with several kinds of wireless link can choose and change between them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each border router builds a tunnel interface towards every enterprise it belongs to, so that all the border routers of that enterprise look like neighbours on one link. Addresses are handed down the tree by delegation, or registered by the router that owns them. Older equipment that only knows the old addressing keeps working alongside all of this.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Communications between endpoints in different sites inside an enterprise cross a commons that joins organisational entities with a mutual spirit of cooperation but possibly competing business, social or political interests. Mechanisms that rely on feedback from routers on the path can therefore become brittle or open to spoofing, because IP packets can be lost to congestion or filtering gateways and because source addresses can be forged. Packets can also be generated by anonymous attackers, for example from a rogue node inside a third-party enterprise with malicious intent.

Path MTU Discovery is an example of a mechanism that relies on ICMP feedback from routers on the path and is therefore exposed to these problems. For IPv4 the common workaround is to disable Path MTU Discovery and let fragmentation occur; for IPv6, where the network does not fragment, the usual mitigation is to discard ICMP messages that do not carry enough information or to work with the minimum IPv6 path MTU.

The architecture does support effective mitigations for distributed denial-of-service and traffic amplification attacks. With VET and SEAL, border gateways can use the 32-bit identification encoded in the SEAL header along with ingress filtering to decide whether a message really came from a topologically correct enterprise across the commons, which lets enterprises apply mitigations at their borders without needing the cooperation of other enterprises. Where source address spoofing by an on-path attacker inside the commons is a concern, tunnel-mode IPsec between the border routers of the enterprises can be used. Border routers obtain provider-independent prefixes through arrangements with a prefix delegation authority and then announce or withdraw them inside the enterprise with router advertisements, which can be signed with SEcure Neighbor Discovery where stronger authentication is needed. The document notes that RANGER does not itself address security considerations, but proposes an architectural framework for specifications that do, and points to a separate document on security concerns with IP tunnelling.
sections.plainLanguage: Because a tunnel crosses a commons whose members may compete with each other, the receiving side checks that the packet really came from the enterprise it claims. The counter in the SEAL header, together with ingress filtering, is what makes that check possible without any cooperation from the other side.

messages.note: The node asks which routing locator reaches the destination's endpoint identifier.

messages.note: The reply names the egress tunnel endpoint, and the node adds it to its forwarding table.

messages.note: The inner packet is wrapped in an outer header addressed to that routing locator.
